subject: ba
title: The Role of Government in Business
objectives: Analyse the objectives of government regulation of business.
Evaluate the roles government plays: Regulator, Participant, and Facilitator.
Identify specific ways the Nigerian government aids business development.
Understand the roles of key agencies including CAC, SON, NAFDAC, BOI and NFIU.
study:
In Nigeria, government relates to business in three ways at once — as a referee setting the rules, a coach providing support, and sometimes as a player running enterprises directly. Government regulates business to protect consumers from fake goods, ensure fair competition, promote economic stability, and protect the environment — while also preventing monopolistic exploitation and guaranteeing essential services the market might otherwise neglect.

Key termThe three categories of government's role in business — Participatory (direct investment in enterprises, e.g. NNPC), Regulatory (registration, import supervision, price control), and Facilitating (incentives and infrastructure that make business easier).

Under its participatory role, government invests directly — wholly owned enterprises in strategic sectors, majority equity stakes, or indirect investment through institutions like NNPC. Under its regulatory role, every business must register with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), imports are inspected before shipment, and price controls have historically been used to curb inflation. Under its facilitating role, government uses tax incentives, fosters competition (through banking reform, commercialisation and privatisation), and shapes fiscal and monetary policy to stimulate investment.

Exam tipLearn to sort real-world examples into the right category on sight: owning NNPC = participatory; requiring CAC registration = regulatory; offering Pioneer Status tax holidays = facilitating.

Specific tools Nigeria has used to support business include commercialisation (running parastatals on a self-financing commercial basis rather than government subvention), privatisation (selling government shareholdings to the public), deregulation (relaxing control, as with the downstream petroleum sector), and Pioneer Status — tax holidays granted to qualifying new industries.

Several agencies do the practical work: the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) handles company registration under CAMA (its registries opened in 1991); the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) sets and enforces product quality standards; NAFDAC regulates the manufacture, import, export, advertisement, distribution and sale of food, drugs, cosmetics, medical devices and chemicals; the Bank of Industry (BOI), Nigeria's oldest development finance institution, provides long-term financing to industrialise the country; and the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) receives and analyses financial intelligence to combat money laundering and terrorism financing. The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), formed in 1971, campaigns for 'Made in Nigeria' goods and represents manufacturers' interests to government.
recap:
• Government's three roles: Participatory (owns enterprises), Regulatory (sets/enforces rules), Facilitating (incentives and infrastructure).
  • Regulation objectives: protect consumers, ensure fair competition, promote stability, protect the environment.
  • Tools: commercialisation, privatisation, deregulation, Pioneer Status tax holidays, fiscal/monetary policy.
  • CAC = company registration · SON = quality standards · NAFDAC = food/drugs/chemicals safety · BOI = long-term industrial financing · NFIU = anti–money laundering intelligence · MAN = manufacturers' advocacy.
